screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will perform four practical skills that matter in a professional environment. First, you will explain the Shared Responsibility Model and precisely describe which controls AWS manages and which controls you, as the customer, must implement. That clarity helps define audit scope and prevents compliance gaps. Second, you will locate and retrieve AWS compliance documents from AWS Artifact and use them during audits to show AWS’s security posture. Third, you will configure AWS Audit Manager to automatically collect evidence against a regulatory framework, reducing manual evidence gathering. Fourth, you will design automated governance using Control Tower and AWS Config Rules to enforce and detect policy violations across multiple accounts. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify skill: explain ownership in a design review, download Artifact reports for a compliance package, run an Audit Manager assessment, and author a Config Rule or enable a Control Tower guardrail. These tasks are practical: they directly reduce audit time, lower risk, and provide documented evidence for your compliance team. Think about which objective you want to practice first in your environment.

screens.title: Shared Responsibility Model
screens.narratorSegment: The Shared Responsibility Model is the foundational definition you must apply to every compliance decision in AWS. It states that AWS manages the security of the cloud — the physical infrastructure, host hardware, and the services themselves — while you, the customer, are responsible for security in the cloud: your data, application code, operating systems, network configuration, and identity and access management. A concrete example: AWS will patch and maintain the hypervisor and the physical data center, but you must configure and rotate KMS keys, enable encryption for S3 buckets, and manage IAM policies for your users. A common misconception is to assume that an AWS compliance certification automatically makes your workload compliant. Certifications only document AWS’s controls; they do not cover your application code, configuration mistakes, or data classification decisions. To make this practical, produce a short ownership matrix for a workload showing which controls are AWS’s and which are your team’s across compute, storage, networking, and identity. Key takeaway: clarity on ownership narrows audit scope, highlights where to focus remediation, and prevents surprises during assessments. Which responsibilities in your design currently lack a named owner?

keyIdea.title: Ownership clarity
keyIdea.text: Shared Responsibility separates infrastructure responsibilities (AWS) from customer responsibilities (configuration, data, and identity).

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › Shared Responsibility
Definition

Shared Responsibility Model

A framework dividing responsibility for security between AWS and the customer.

AWS is responsible for
  • Physical infrastructure and global network
  • Host and hypervisor security
  • Managed service availability and isolation
You are responsible for
  • Data, encryption, and key management
  • OS, application config, and IAM
  • Network configuration and security groups
Key Takeaway

Document ownership for each control area to avoid compliance gaps during audits.

Analogy

Think of AWS as the building and utilities; you are responsible for the content of your office and its locks.

Example Task
Create an ownership matrix across Compute, Storage, Network, and Identity showing who patches, who configures encryption, and who audits logs.
Common Mistake

Assuming AWS certifications remove your need to secure data and manage configurations.

screens.title: AWS Artifact — source of compliance reports
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Artifact is the repository you will use when auditors ask for AWS’s compliance documentation. It provides on-demand access to AWS security and compliance reports and selected agreements. Typical documents found in Artifact include ISO certifications, PCI DSS attestations, SOC reports, and HIPAA Business Associate Addendums. These documents are evidence of the controls AWS runs and are useful during your audits to show the boundary of what AWS manages. A concrete example is attaching a SOC report from Artifact to your application’s audit packet to demonstrate AWS’s control environment for infrastructure. A frequent misconception is treating Artifact documents as proof that your entire solution is compliant. They only prove AWS’s responsibilities. You still must provide evidence for your controls: encryption settings, IAM configurations, and monitoring outputs. Practical step: when preparing for an audit, download the relevant Artifact reports and map each report item to a specific control in your assessment. This mapping reduces back-and-forth with auditors and shows that you understand both sides of the responsibility model. AWS Artifact — source of compliance reports means use artifact to obtain aws’s compliance reports and attach them to your audit package to demonstrate aws’s control environment.. In practical terms, how to use artifact as auditor-facing evidence for aws controls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › AWS Artifact
Definition

AWS Artifact

A central resource for on-demand access to AWS compliance reports and select agreements.

Typical documents
  • ISO certifications
  • PCI DSS attestations
  • SOC reports and HIPAA BAA references
Example

Attach a SOC report from Artifact to your audit packet to show infrastructure control coverage.

Practices
  • Download relevant reports before an audit and map them to your controls.
  • Keep copies with your compliance evidence and note applicable date ranges.
  • Never treat Artifact documents as proof of your configuration or application controls.
Common Mistake

Assuming Artifact reports make your solution compliant without your own evidence.

screens.title: AWS Audit Manager — automating evidence collection
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Audit Manager automates much of the evidence collection required for auditing against frameworks such as PCI DSS, HIPAA, or GDPR. Think of it as a service that maps technical artifacts — configuration snapshots, CloudTrail logs, Security Hub findings — to control requirements in a selected framework. A practical example: choose the PCI DSS pre-built framework and run an assessment; Audit Manager will continuously collect evidence from supported services and assemble it into auditor-friendly reports. This reduces manual evidence gathering and the risk of missing items before an audit. When using Audit Manager, decide upfront which evidence sources you will trust, how often evidence is collected, and who will review findings. A common misconception is that Audit Manager fixes non-compliance automatically — it organizes and presents evidence, but you still need remediation actions for findings. To operate effectively, combine Audit Manager with Config Rules and a documented remediation playbook so evidence that shows non-compliance leads to tracked fixes. Closing question: which evidence sources in your environment would you connect to an Audit Manager assessment first? AWS Audit Manager — automating evidence collection means audit manager maps aws service outputs to control requirements and produces continuous, auditor-friendly evidence collections.. In practical terms, set up assessments and map evidence to frameworks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › Audit Manager
Process

Set up an assessment

1
Choose a framework
Select a pre-built framework such as PCI DSS, HIPAA, or GDPR to map controls automatically.
2
Connect evidence sources
Point Audit Manager to Config, CloudTrail, Security Hub, and other sources to collect evidence continuously.
3
Review and report
Use auditor-friendly reports and track findings. Export evidence for your auditor when needed.
Example

Run a PCI DSS assessment and have Audit Manager collect evidence from Config rules that check encryption and from CloudTrail for access logs.

Pro Tip

Define who reviews evidence items and how remediation is tracked so that Audit Manager feeds into an operational process, not just a report.

Misconception

Audit Manager organizes evidence but does not remediate resources automatically; pair it with Config or automation for fixes.

screens.title: AWS Control Tower and guardrails
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Control Tower is the practical service for establishing a governed, multi-account AWS landing zone. It automates the setup of core accounts such as management, log archive, and audit, configures AWS Organizations, and deploys a set of guardrails. Guardrails are either preventive controls, implemented as service control policies, or detective controls, often implemented with Config Rules. For example, a preventive guardrail can block creation of publicly accessible S3 buckets, while a detective guardrail will flag unencrypted EBS volumes. When designing governance, take a layered approach: Control Tower for account structure and baseline guardrails, Config Rules for continuous configuration checks, and centralized logging to the log archive account so auditors can review immutable records. A common pitfall is leaving existing accounts unmanaged — either enroll them into Control Tower or ensure equivalent guardrails are applied consistently. Key design question: which preventive controls must be enforced automatically versus detected and remediated after the fact? That decision drives whether you implement an SCP or a Config remediation workflow. AWS Control Tower and guardrails means control tower automates a secure multi-account landing zone and deploys guardrails to enforce preventive and detective controls at scale.. In practical terms, establishing multi-account governance and preventive/detective controls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Control Tower automates a secure multi-account landing zone and deploys guardrails to enforce preventive and detective controls at scale.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › Control Tower
What it does

Control Tower landing zone

  • Automates account factory and core accounts
  • Configures AWS Organizations at baseline
  • Deploys guardrails (prevention and detection)
Example guardrails
Prevent public S3; detect unencrypted EBS; require logging and centralized logs.
Design notes

Decide which controls must be preventive (implemented by SCPs) and which can be detective (Config Rules with remediation).

Operational tip

Enroll existing accounts or apply equivalent guardrails to avoid inconsistent security posture.

Common Mistake

Assuming Control Tower replaces all governance controls — it sets a baseline and must be complemented by Config Rules and remediation processes.

screens.title: AWS Config Rules — continuous configuration checks
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Config Rules continuously evaluate resource configurations against desired baselines and flag non-compliant resources. They are essential for continuous compliance because they provide automatic detection of drift and a place to trigger remediation or alerts. An example from the chapter is the managed rule encrypted-volumes, which marks any unencrypted EBS volume as non-compliant whenever its configuration changes. When a Config Rule marks a resource as non-compliant, you can configure notifications or automated remediation, shortening the time to fix issues. A typical misconception is thinking Config Rules both detect and fully resolve complex architectural non-compliance without additional tooling; for many cases, Config Rules are best paired with automation scripts, Lambda functions, or Systems Manager Automation to remediate. To be effective, maintain a library of rules aligned to your chosen frameworks and review them periodically. Key takeaway: Config Rules make compliance continuous and measurable, and they are the detective half of many Control Tower guardrails. Ask yourself which rules should run across all accounts by default versus those applied only to workload accounts. AWS Config Rules — continuous configuration checks means config rules provide ongoing evaluation of resource state and a structured path to alerts and remediation for non-compliant resources.. In practical terms, detect non-compliant resources and trigger remediation paths. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › AWS Config Rules
Capability

Continuous configuration evaluation

Rules evaluate resources on configuration change and periodically to identify drift from desired state.

Example rule
A managed rule named encrypted-volumes checks whether EBS volumes are encrypted and marks unencrypted volumes non-compliant.
Remediation

Use notifications and automated remediation pipelines when a rule detects non-compliance. Pair rules with playbooks for human review when needed.

Pitfall

Not acting on findings leads to compliance drift. Schedule regular reviews of rule results and remediation status.

screens.title: Config Rule example — encrypted EBS volumes
screens.narratorSegment: Here we walk through the concrete example mentioned in the chapter: a managed AWS Config Rule that checks whether Amazon EBS volumes are encrypted. The rule is typically enabled from the Config console or via infrastructure-as-code; it triggers on configuration changes and can be run periodically to ensure coverage. The practical effect is that any unencrypted EBS volume will be marked as non-compliant and appear in Config’s findings. A common mistake is assuming that marking non-compliant is the same as remediation — it only signals the issue. For remediation you should document and implement a validated process: either an automated snapshot-and-encrypt pipeline, replace-with-encrypted-volume steps, or an operational ticket with remediation SLAs. Example action: enable the managed rule named encrypted-volumes, verify it finds a non-encrypted volume, and then test your remediation workflow. That proves both detection and fix. Takeaway: detection without defined remediation still leaves data at risk; always pair Config Rules with a remediation plan or automation. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › Encrypted Volumes Rule
Managed rule

encrypted-volumes

# Example: AWS Config managed rule
# Rule Name: encrypted-volumes
# Description: Checks whether Amazon EBS volumes are encrypted.
# Trigger: On configuration changes and periodic evaluations
# Action: Marks unencrypted EBS volumes as NON_COMPLIANT
Test

Enable the managed rule and create a non-encrypted EBS volume to verify the rule marks it non-compliant.

Remediation options
  • Automated snapshot + create encrypted volume
  • Replace volume in maintenance window
  • Raise operational ticket with SLA
Common Mistake

Assuming detection equates to remediation; document and test the remediation path.

screens.title: Industry compliance: HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR
screens.narratorSegment: Industry and regional standards drive different architectural choices. HIPAA emphasizes protection of protected health information by requiring encryption at rest and in transit, strict access controls, detailed audit logging, and incident response capabilities. For HIPAA you will commonly use KMS for key management, S3 with SSE-KMS, CloudTrail for logging, GuardDuty for threat detection, and a formal incident response plan. PCI DSS focuses on protecting cardholder data and often requires network segmentation, strong access controls, encryption, vulnerability management, and regular security testing; typical services include VPC segmentation, security groups, WAF, Shield, KMS, and Config Rules. GDPR centers on data privacy, consent, and data subject rights and therefore emphasizes data residency, minimization, and the ability to remove or export a subject’s data. screens.title: Data Residency and Sovereignty
screens.narratorSegment: Data residency and data sovereignty are often decisive constraints when you design cloud architectures. Data residency refers to the physical location where data is stored, and data sovereignty refers to the legal jurisdictions that apply to that data. AWS supports region selection so you can keep data within national borders if required. In practice, Solutions Architects address these requirements by deploying isolated stacks in the permitted regions and avoiding cross-region transfers unless they are explicitly allowed and secured. For example, a European healthcare workload bound by local laws may require all datasets and backups to remain in an EU region; you would therefore provision separate accounts and services in those regions and ensure CloudTrail logs and backups are also stored in-region. A common pitfall is accidental cross-region replication or central logging that violates residency rules; auditing and organization-wide guardrails prevent such mistakes. Key takeaway: treat residency and sovereignty as hard architecture constraints and document acceptable cross-region patterns with legal counsel before you implement them. Data Residency and Sovereignty means treat data residency and sovereignty as architecture constraints: deploy isolated stacks in allowed regions and avoid unsanctioned cross-region transfers.. In practical terms, choosing regions and isolating stacks for legal and regulatory requirements. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Lab: Monitor IMDSv2 enforcement with AWS Config
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks you through monitoring Instance Metadata enforcement using AWS Config. Start by ensuring Config is enabled in your account and has the appropriate recording settings. Next, create a Config Rule by searching for the managed rule named ec2-imdsv2-enabled and enable it; this rule detects EC2 instances that do not enforce Instance Metadata Service Version 2. Four steps to detect EC2 instances that do not enforce IMDSv2.

IMDSv2 reduces metadata attack surface. Detecting instances without it protects credentials and metadata-based attacks.

screens.title: Common mistakes and governance anti-patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Organizations commonly make several governance mistakes that lead to compliance drift. One frequent error is misunderstanding the Shared Responsibility Model and assuming AWS certifications absolve the customer of securing their configurations. Another is relying on a static set of Config Rules and never reviewing or updating them as services or regulations evolve. Multi-account environments often suffer from inconsistent baselines when teams avoid Control Tower or fail to enroll existing accounts; this results in gaps and extra audit work. A typical operational failure is collecting Audit Manager findings but not tracking remediation to closure, which leaves persistent risk. Prevent these issues by documenting ownership, automating detection via Config Rules and Control Tower guardrails, creating runbooks for remediation, and using Audit Manager to collect evidence while ensuring findings feed into tracked tickets or automation. A short practical habit: schedule a quarterly compliance review that checks Config Rule results, Audit Manager evidence, and enrollment status for new accounts. That practice helps catch drift early and keeps auditors satisfied. In this lesson we will build a clear mental model for cloud compliance and governance using services AWS provides. You will leave understanding the shared responsibility model and how it affects what you must secure, how to use AWS Artifact and Audit Manager to collect evidence, and the automated guardrails and rules that let organizations stay compliant continuously. We’ll also examine how to address data residency and industry-specific standards like HIPAA, PCI DSS, and GDPR. I’ll give concrete examples you can use in design reviews, including a hands-on scenario to monitor Instance Metadata enforcement. This knowledge matters because compliance is not a one-time checklist — it is an architecture constraint that affects account structure, logging, encryption, and operations. Throughout, watch for common mistakes such as assuming AWS certifications remove your responsibilities or letting compliance drift by not acting on Audit Manager findings. By the end you’ll be able to name which AWS service provides audit reports, how to automate evidence collection, and which governance constructs you should use in a multi-account environment. Consider which compliance requirement in your environment would be most impacted by an automated Config Rule.

By the end of this chapter you will perform four practical skills that matter in a professional environment. First, you will explain the Shared Responsibility Model and precisely describe which controls AWS manages and which controls you, as the customer, must implement. That clarity helps define audit scope and prevents compliance gaps. Second, you will locate and retrieve AWS compliance documents from AWS Artifact and use them during audits to show AWS’s security posture. Third, you will configure AWS Audit Manager to automatically collect evidence against a regulatory framework, reducing manual evidence gathering. Fourth, you will design automated governance using Control Tower and AWS Config Rules to enforce and detect policy violations across multiple accounts. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify skill: explain ownership in a design review, download Artifact reports for a compliance package, run an Audit Manager assessment, and author a Config Rule or enable a Control Tower guardrail. These tasks are practical: they directly reduce audit time, lower risk, and provide documented evidence for your compliance team. Think about which objective you want to practice first in your environment.

This screen maps each objective to an actionable milestone you can complete. For shared responsibility, the milestone is to produce a one-page ownership diagram that auditors and engineers can sign off on; include who configures encryption, who manages OS patching, and who monitors network controls. For Artifact and audit evidence, your milestone is to download at least two AWS compliance reports such as SOC or ISO from AWS Artifact and attach them to a sample audit packet. For Audit Manager, the milestone is to create and run an assessment using a pre-built framework and review the automatically collected evidence to identify gaps. For governance, the milestone is to enable a Control Tower landing zone or at minimum author and enable an AWS Config Rule and document its remediation path. Each milestone reduces manual effort or increases assurance. These steps are small, testable, and designed to show auditors tangible proof. Choose one milestone to practice now and record what changed in your environment so your next review has less surprise.

The Shared Responsibility Model is the foundational definition you must apply to every compliance decision in AWS. It states that AWS manages the security of the cloud — the physical infrastructure, host hardware, and the services themselves — while you, the customer, are responsible for security in the cloud: your data, application code, operating systems, network configuration, and identity and access management. A concrete example: AWS will patch and maintain the hypervisor and the physical data center, but you must configure and rotate KMS keys, enable encryption for S3 buckets, and manage IAM policies for your users. A common misconception is to assume that an AWS compliance certification automatically makes your workload compliant. Certifications only document AWS’s controls; they do not cover your application code, configuration mistakes, or data classification decisions. To make this practical, produce a short ownership matrix for a workload showing which controls are AWS’s and which are your team’s across compute, storage, networking, and identity. Key takeaway: clarity on ownership narrows audit scope, highlights where to focus remediation, and prevents surprises during assessments. Which responsibilities in your design currently lack a named owner?

AWS Artifact is the repository you will use when auditors ask for AWS’s compliance documentation. It provides on-demand access to AWS security and compliance reports and selected agreements. Typical documents found in Artifact include ISO certifications, PCI DSS attestations, SOC reports, and HIPAA Business Associate Addendums. These documents are evidence of the controls AWS runs and are useful during your audits to show the boundary of what AWS manages. A concrete example is attaching a SOC report from Artifact to your application’s audit packet to demonstrate AWS’s control environment for infrastructure. A frequent misconception is treating Artifact documents as proof that your entire solution is compliant. They only prove AWS’s responsibilities. You still must provide evidence for your controls: encryption settings, IAM configurations, and monitoring outputs. Practical step: when preparing for an audit, download the relevant Artifact reports and map each report item to a specific control in your assessment. This mapping reduces back-and-forth with auditors and shows that you understand both sides of the responsibility model. Organizations commonly make several governance mistakes that lead to compliance drift. One frequent error is misunderstanding the Shared Responsibility Model and assuming AWS certifications absolve the customer of securing their configurations. These are the core ideas to keep top of mind. Second, AWS Artifact is where you obtain AWS’s compliance reports and agreements to demonstrate AWS’s control environment during audits. Third, Audit Manager automates evidence collection by mapping service outputs to control requirements and delivering auditor-friendly reports. Fourth, Control Tower and guardrails create a governed multi-account baseline, using SCPs for prevention and Config Rules for detection. Fifth, Config Rules provide continuous checks and must be paired with remediation processes.
